utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If there's no procedural issue to be raised, I'd like to turn into closed session again in order to continue the cross-examination of Witness 666. We'll turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, unless you would object to that, I would first like to ask Madam Registrar to deal with the exhibits that have been presented to Witness 666 and then have them -- and then to determine whether they are admitted, yes or no. And if there's any remaining issue, then you may address us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With one preliminary matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- and that is that the video of the funeral was not shown in court, but a still from that video was. And secondly, a transcript of a speech given at that -- at the time of that funeral was. So what we wish to do was to actually have the video footage presented as part of Exhibit 17, even though it was not presented to the witness. When I -- when I say "17", it's not exhibit 17 but it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's number 17 on the exhibit list presented in relation to Witness 666. Mr. Stewart, would there be any ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, a reasonable question would be, Why? After all, it seems but a waste of time. If -- I wouldn't have checked if the Prosecution indicate what possible point was to be got out of this video in addition to all the evidence that's been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If there is a point, then all right. But it's a bit mysterious what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, what would the video add to what is on paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the video will depict where the individual depicted in the still was standing at the time that the still had been made and will give context to that exhibit. The video will depict a relevant issue raised in the Defence's examination of the number of people present, the nature of the people present at the funeral. The video also will depict not only the words spoken by Radovan Karadzic but to who he spoke those words and the atmosphere at the time he spoke those words, which was also another subject of the witness's evidence. And furthermore, just from a practical point of view, we would be putting it in as a contextual document. Otherwise, it just wouldn't be convenient if the video footage itself was separated from the still and the transcript that have been introduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, any --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, well, the still was a different occasion altogether, so that's not really nothing to do with it. It's impossible to understand what the practical inconveniences of separating the video footage from the evidence. One just doesn't put the video footage in. But the really important point is this: It appears that some point will be made about the -- by the Prosecution in relation to the physical location of individuals on this occasion. Your Honour, that should have been introduced in evidence when the witness was giving his evidence in chief because if there is any point at all of any relevance of at arising from the video, then it was clearly a matter which should have been open to cross-examination when the witness was here. So there are two courses now: Forget the video, because the evidence is there as it stands; or let's see the video played, and let's bring the witness back, then, for any further cross-examination required in relation to that matter. But it must be one or other of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the evidence that the witness has given in relation to the funeral, we do not think will be added to by him viewing the video. However, the circumstances of the funeral, the capacity of Your Honours to assess the evidence that has been given by the witness will be added to by the video, and we reiterate that to have this separated from the other exhibits, which are derived from the video, would be an unnecessary creation of separate exhibit number and unnecessary administrative difficulties. I am certain that the video itself is a piece of evidence that is relevant to this proceeding, and for that very reason - - on many occasions there was reference to what took place at this funeral throughout the witness's evidence, but there would be no need to bring him back to make any further comment than the comments he has already made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I may take it that the video was disclosed to the Defence well in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not the point though. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was my question. The question of fact. Whether it's a point or not, I just wanted to satisfy myself whether this video was in the hands of the Defence at a due time. Let me just consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there anything more to be said in this respect? We heard from the Defence; we heard from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, please understand, Your Honour, I wasn't contradicting or intending to undermine in any way Your Honour's factual inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was simply trying to develop it. That doesn't - - the point goes beyond that. It's this: Your Honour, this video was not -- was not introduced in evidence. It was supplied to the Defence. But we -- if the Prosecution do not put something in evidence, then we decide in the light of their not putting it in evidence not to use it. But they are now after the witness has left court seeking to put this in evidence for some extra purpose, and it -- it therefore must -- it's -- it must be adding to the evidence because if it doesn't add to the evidence, there's no possible reason for it to go in. So they are seeking to add to the evidence after the witness has left court. The evidence that the Prosecution put in is evidence on which I must be entitled to cross- examine. So that is -- it's the same choice, Your Honour, I indicated a moment ago: It either stays out, or if they are going to show it, we should all see it now and the witness should see it -- not necessarily for him to add a comment in chief. That's in the Prosecution's hands whether they invite him to add any comment. But for me then to ask him any questions in cross-examination that arise out of that. Because up until the point when the witness left court, this video had not been put in evidence and exhibit numbers certainly -- Your Honour, the idea that exhibit numbering overrides the proper decisions on what evidence should or shouldn't be admitted is pretty far-fetched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The video will be admitted into evidence. It allows the Chamber to verify some of the answers given by the witness, also some of the answers given in cross-examination. At least, the Chamber expects that the video could insist in that respect. Any further issue in respect of this, Mr. Margetts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Madam Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, when does the Trial Chamber view such a video?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will view this video in its chambers, and to the extent it becomes relevant, the Chamber will find a way of informing the public about this piece of evidence being admitted and about the content of it because that's one of the requirements for a public trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that -- that would have to be linked in then, wouldn't it, Your Honour, with respect, with the fact that the whole of this witness's evidence has been dealt with in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree with you. I'd forgotten about protective measures; although, it may well be that this video is not in need of admission under seal. But we'll have a look at that first, and we'll -- there's no need to admit it under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. This is not admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll find a way to make this an exhibit accessible to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I do understand that you'd like to address the Chamber. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask for the Prosecution, if possible, to give me that tape so that I can take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it -- yes, whether that's for the Prosecution, or whether you should look at the video as it has been provided to the Defence. I would avoid that everything has to be provided double, but it's for sure, Mr. Krajisnik, that you should have an opportunity to look at the tape. As a matter of fact, not only after today, but since it has been disclosed to the Defence, it was accessible already, and as you know, the Chamber does not interfere with the internal communication of the Defence. But certainly if you ask Mr. Stewart, he'll certainly give you an opportunity to look at the -- I don't know whether it's on a CD or whether it's on a tape. But you'll find a way to look at it. I take it, Mr. Stewart, that this is ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. The -- the reason I didn't -- the same thought was going through my mind as Mr. Krajisnik's, which I'm happy to say does occasionally happen. But the same question had gone on in my mind: I didn't ask it simply because it's a matter that I had in mind I would clear up with Mr. Krajisnik just to find out from a practical point of view whether he had viewed the video. Because Your Honour is quite right; the internal arrangements come into it. But Your Honour, I must emphasise once again the practical reality of this case is such that -- the supposed theoretical smooth-running of the matters so that all these matters can be viewed by everybody in time to deal with the witnesses: this Trial Chamber has made that smooth process impossible for us by the schedule adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I just interrupt you. How much time does the video take?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's approximately -- there's two segments. One of approximately 30 seconds and a second segment of approximately three and a half minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the witness is -- let me turn first into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The video being played, would there be any need to put further questions to the witness, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I would like to do - and it's why I've asked Mr. Karganovic to come back into court for the moment - I would like to just very quickly confer with Mr. Krajisnik and then see, but I expect that to take one minute, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Take that one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's absolutely no problem, and we -- well, we don't know what the Prosecution seek to get out of that, but we have no request to bring the witness back and no further comment or question to make in -- in relation to that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Well, what the Prosecution did seek was already explained by Mr. Margetts. There's no need for repetition to that. Madam Registrar, could we then assign an exhibit number to this in relation to the transcript of the text spoken on this video.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will be Prosecution Exhibit 877, and the transcript will be P877A, which is found at tab 17 of the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you then, please, give us the numbers of the documents that have been tendered into evidence until now and tell us what should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P866, under seal. P867, under seal. P868, under seal. P869, under seal. P870, under seal. P871. P872. P873, under seal. P874. P875. P876, under seal. P877 and P877A. And P880.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Since I hear no objections, these exhibits are admitted into evidence. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Perhaps you would like add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There -- the documents that appear in the presentation binder at tabs 8, 9, 10, and 14 are submitted by the Prosecution as contextual documents in regard to this particular area of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, would you please assign exhibit numbers to it. And as usual, contextual exhibits, within one week we'd like to hear about any objections, and therefore they are provisionally admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need to have any of them under seal, or could they all --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, would you then please read the description and assign the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document found at tab 8, P-- will be P881, order for combat activities, dated the 7th of June, 1992. P881A is the document found at tab 9, daily operative report from Birac Brigade command, dated 14 June 1992. P881B, located at tab 10, Andric request to the command of the East Bosnia Corps, dated 14 June 1992. And finally, P881C, located at tab 14, information on prisoners, dated 03 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Apologies. There's one further matter in regard to these exhibits. Your Honour noted an error in the translation of the document appearing at tab 12, which is Exhibit P874. We have rectified that translation, and we have the corrected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, is this the numbering, et cetera? I think I corrected it by hand. Parties are invited to do the same. And it's -- I should have told you immediately, Mr. Margetts, because that would have saved you the work and that would have saved us the paper to be copied. I apologise for not having done it, but I have already corrected the one-and-only original version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And your correction stands in the transcript, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Usually if I make any correction to an original document, even if it's a translation, I always refer to the date of the transcript in which we dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. There is one further matter, and that is that the Prosecution has noted that there was some ambiguity in one of the words utilised in Exhibits P881 and P881A, and we have rectified the translation, and we'll distribute those. They are contextual documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd please take care that they'll be distributed and that ... Mr. Usher, could you please assist. Mr. Tieger, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Ms. Richterova will be leading the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: However, as long as we are engaged in the process of assigning exhibit numbers, I wanted to raise one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- very brief matter in connection with an issue that arose during the cross-examination of Witness 165.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the discussion concerning how those issues could be clarified and whether any documents should be tendered into evidence in connection with it. I have spoken with Ms. Loukas about that. The parties agree that the indictment and judgement of Mr. Vuckovic should be tendered into evidence, and I have those with me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll ask Madam Registrar to assign exhibit numbers to them, as well. That's in relation to Witness 165. Yes, Madam Registrar, I think you were not -- I think no numbers have yet been assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they're two new exhibits. Would they be Prosecution exhibits or Defence exhibits or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll undertake the burden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar will -- if you'd please give them to Madam Registrar. Then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think it should be -- I mean, the witness was -- there's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My recollection is there were protective measures in place and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But in view of the character of these documents, I don't think that there would be any need to tender them under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I shouldn't think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's helpful for the Court's scheduling, I note that we would require approximately three to five minutes to distribute documents to the booth before actually beginning the examination of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd start with it immediately, then we could start with the witness in five minutes from now. Meanwhile --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And meanwhile, we are still about to distribute the other documents, and Madam Registrar will assign the exhibit numbers to the exhibits related to 165.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just add this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I have a moment to speak to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- Ms. Richterova, it might save a little bit of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So during those five minute, I'll endeavour to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, wouldn't it be the best that we resume after five minutes. --- Break taken at 12.11 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, numbers still to be assigned to the contextual exhibits? No, we have done that. We have done that. Yes. Then we have -- no, numbers to be assigned to the two additional exhibits in relation to Witness 165.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The indictment dated 28 April 1994 will be Prosecution Exhibit P882. The registry has only received the English translation of the document. The document entitled "In the name of the people," ERN number 00477911, will be P883.1, and the original will be P883.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I think that the Defence used only the English version of the indictment. I don't know whether you used the indictment, but at least some of the documents. Is there any need to also have the original in B/C/S in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's no need to have it in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I suppose if we need to look at it with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And our thanks to Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And Madam Registrar, that means that no original is required for P882. Then are you ready, Ms. Richterova, to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought into the courtroom -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I just say, Your Honour, that I've said Ms. Richterova can lead this witness in her entirety. There may come a point where I'll object to that, in which case I'll get up and make it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But at the moment I don't object to any leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. I noticed that this morning's session will end after another 65 minutes of examination time because we need another break in view of the tapes. It's up to the parties whether they think they could manage to finish the examination of this witness this morning. Otherwise, we'll continue at 3.00 this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good day, Ms. Malesevic, if I'm well informed. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Malesevic, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll first be examined by Ms. Richterova, counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Richterova, you may proceed. Examined by Ms. Richterova:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Malesevic. I will ask you a few questions about your background, or better say I will read the background information and at the end if you could confirm whether our informations are correct. You were born on 15 of September, 1949, in Jajce. You attended a secondary technical school in Jajce. You started studying Faculty of Economy of their university, of the Banja Luka University; however, you finished only two years of your study. And after that, you started working in the field of economy as a bookkeeper, head of bookkeeping department, and until the war started, you were head of export department of one company in Jajce; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just clarify. I was at the construction company involved in the export of those services. We did construction work abroad, so I was involved in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In October 1992, after Jajce was taken over by VRS soldiers, you went to Travnik and then further to Kresevo. And from 19 June 1993 until 22nd of March, 1994, you were in camp in Kresevo, and this camp was run by Croatian authority; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were released from the camp, you went first to Visoko and then you went to Sarajevo. And in 1995, you were involved in the work of Committee for Women, which was a humanitarian organisation; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from 25 of August, 1996, you were a secretary of the Bosnian National Alliance of Associations for Former Camp Inmates; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you worked in this association or in this alliance as a secretary.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you very briefly tell us what were your duties as a secretary in this alliance.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me start at the beginning. I participated in the setting-up of the association of former camp inmates of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Initially we had quite a few problems. We had to organise the association on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to get the data as soon as possible, the number of former inmates, the places where they were held, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you speak probably too quickly for the interpreters. But before we will continue, may I ask you, and, in fact, it was supposed to be my first question: This alliance, what was the main object of work of this alliance?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: The main aims and priorities of the work of the alliance was gathering information about the places of imprisonment and the number of inmates that were held in those camps between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that before the alliance was set up, there were other associations of camp inmates?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And upon their initiative, in order to pool all the documents, we decided to set up the alliance in order to have it all in one place. It followed the initiative of the other associations that had been set up prior to the setting-up of the alliance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that the prime goal was - and I think you already mentioned it - to have a complete evidence of detention facilities on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the main aim of the setting-up of the alliance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that you collected information not only on detention facilities which were run by the Serbian authorities but also run by Bosnian and Croat -- Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We gathered all information, no matter whose control those facilities were under.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've -- I'm not quite sure whether now is the time for the break or whether the break ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'll leave it a bit up to you. We should have a break, a break of 20 minutes, which should start anything from now until ten minutes from now. So if this would be a suitable moment, we'd have a break now. Otherwise, if you'd like to put a few more questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will put a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But not later than 20 to 1.00, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At this moment, I would like to show the witness an exhibit, which is called "inmates dossier". We have -- we have it in English and original language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It should be in the package under tab number 2 -- oh, I'm sorry, we do not have it. It should be under the witness statement in the dossier. Can we ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The inmate's dossier, it is ERN number, last three digits, 692 and following; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Up to and including 820 in the -- no, that's the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it goes until 705 in the English translation and then original B/C/S, last three digits, 808 until 820.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: That's exactly right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you started working on creation of this complete evidence or list of all detention facilities, is it right that you interviewed people who claimed that they were detained in any of these detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did talk to them, but the forms we used in the past were not altogether transparent, so to say, and that has led to a need for a more comprehensive and a more exhaustive kind of form in order for us to be able to ascertain data properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the -- the -- if you say that more exhaustive kind of form, is this form which is in front of you the kind of form you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: It is. Initially we would simply look at certificates issued by the International Red Cross Committee and the state Committee, but it proved to be insufficient because there was not sufficient data in there. So after -- slightly longer than a year, we managed to compile a dossier of former inmates, and there are about 56 basic questions, it seems to me, and 270-something sub-questions. So we've got more 300 questions, which should be providing answers to everything that we were interested in at that particular moment in time in order to be able to have a complete picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You tend to speak very quickly. Could I ask you to slow down; otherwise, it could not be translated. We would not hear what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we don't need to go into too many details regarding this form because the Judges can read it by themselves. However, I want to mention one thing, which is, You were not collecting information only on places of detention, but also you were collecting information on the way how they were treated; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: It is. Apart from identifying the detention facilities where they were held, we were interested in the kind of treatment that was dispensed to them, so that we asked for detailed descriptions of the treatment, starting from food, hygiene, and so on and so forth, and what sort of abuse happened in those detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned what sort of abuse, did you create any special report or list which would refer only to the way how people were abused in -- in camps?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of the dossiers which identified various forms of abuse, we then compiled a kind of set of documents, which was published -- it was called the Book of Torture, and we did it on the basis of authentic statements, and we listed more than 80 various basic types of abuse without any nuances on the basis of copies we kept at our centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- and very briefly because we have heard lots of testimonies of witnesses who were talking about the way how they were treated in prisons or various camps. Can you tell us just examples of these abuses, two, three, four examples, based on -- on your knowledge, based on the statements you prepared or you read.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just say that the type of murder or killings had 15 different types, such as starvation, shooting, strangulation, et cetera. And then we've heard of detailed accounts of rapes, strangulations, experimenting with people. More than 80 different types of abuse are illustrated in this Book of Torture, which is based on statements of camp inmates who survived. Their teeth were pulled out; their hands and feet were chopped off; they were forced to eat body parts, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Malesevic, now I would like to go back to detention facilities. I would like to know - and it would assist the Judges to know - if a place was proclaimed a detention facility, what kind of proof you asked to be provided.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Since the law in Bosnia and Herzegovina has not provided us with a definition of detention facilities, we agreed on a definition ourselves. So basically any place which was fenced in and there were guards, armed guards there, and people were detained there unlawfully and human rights were being violated, all those places were considered as detention facilities. And on the basis of that, we compiled the list, which we hope will be checked by the international community one day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think this is the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the adjournment, we were talking about the way -- how you declared a certain place a detention facility. When a person wanted to assert a status as camp prisoner, is it correct that such a person had to first contact the municipal association of camp inmates?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Such a person has to provide either a certificate from the International Committee of the Red Cross or other similar body or had to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. bring two witnesses who can testify that he was in that particular camp; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after this information is provided to municipal association, they will verify the accuracy of the information and forward the file to the regional or cantonal association; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they will again verify all the information and finally the file will reach the national alliance association in Sarajevo; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you will again verify all the information.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we would check everything once again, and then we would issue a certificate about the inmate status.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I would like to show and tender into evidence such a certificate, and it is in -- in our dossier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The certificate will be Prosecution Exhibit P885.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you confirm that this is the certificate which is issued by the alliance after all the information provided by a person are verified?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a form that we issue as a certificate that the person in question was indeed detained in one of those camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that during your work, you personally went to the field and verified by yourself or your associates the places which were claimed to be detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very often, in cooperation with the municipal associations, we carried out in-the-field checks very frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the alliance in Sarajevo, you created dossiers per municipalities in which you kept all the files with information provided by prisoners; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: It is. If I may explain. We actually had a classification of camps project. We tried to define all those places according to municipalities, cantons, and regions, and this was the reason why we decided to file documents in that way, in order to make everything more easily accessible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, the -- the main work was done by the municipal associations because they were more familiar with the places; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were in direct contact with the inhabitants of the area and the people who were arrested in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, they always cooperated with -- with the alliance and provided them with all the necessary information.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And all the gathered information was submitted to the alliance for further processing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Malesevic, it is true that you are no longer an employee of the Bosnian National Alliance of Associations and that you left the association in 2004?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you gave -- before you were asked to give testimony here, you had access to files in the alliance.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were able to verify certain information.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Not all information, but some of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: With the permission of -- of Your Honour, I would like to go through the Schedule C of the indictment, and the reason why I was asking for permission is that I know that Mrs. Malesevic has some notes. And as the list is quite long, I would -- I think she will need to consult her notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If it is necessary, we have enough copies of this Schedule C, if Your Honours need it for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not the indictment here with Schedule C on it but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have my indictment at hand, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would have a few copies of Schedule C, that would be ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Malesevic, I would like to go through this list and ask you always a few questions in relation to particular municipality. In Banja Luka, we listed nine places. To your knowledge, are all these places, places of detention?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our document -- documentation, the first eight places are considered places of detention. Number 9, the Borik Stadium, was actually a collection centre in 1995. And I would like to emphasise that under 1.1, the prison in Banja Luka is also known as the Tunjice prison. 1.3, the small camp is actually the military investigations centre. They were all open in 1992, except for the collections centre in Borik, which was open in 1995. The biggest camp in Banja Luka was Manjaca, where there was the largest number of people detained and passed through it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that a camp at Borik was a collection centre. Is it correct to state that a collection centre or collection point is just a place where people were gathered in order to be transferred to other places, so they were kept there only for a short -- for a shorter period of time?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When it comes to the Borik collections centre, I would like to say that this was the place from which people left Banja Luka. It could be called a collections centre. However there, is another collections centre that we will come across. I don't know whether the collections centre could be applied to it because people were brought there by force after every -- they had been robbed, and very often people had to sign a document relinquishing all of their property to Republika Srpska. We called this a collection centre because we did not have any other name. The Borik collection centre is the one that we do not consider a detention centre, and people who were there are not considered detainees; we do not have them on our records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other municipality is Bijeljina. We listed 15 places; to your knowledge, are they all places of detention?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: All the 15 places are considered detention centres, and we have documents for those; most of them were opened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Malesevic, I think we now -- you mentioned collection centres instead of -- and I don't know whether you used this expression, "collection centre," incorrectly or whether they are really -- oh, detention centres. I'm sorry. It's my fault. You -- you count them all detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Detention facilities. And they're all --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May I make one observation, and it's this: Clearly the Court wants to know which of these were open in 1992, and it may be that the witness will need to go through each municipality dealing with 1992. I mean, she just said most of them were open in 1992. I make that observation now because otherwise I will deal with that in cross- examination, but it would probably be duplication of what needs to be done, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If what I've said is not helpful, then I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could also approach it negatively, which were not opened, or opened only after 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. In fact, I - - I meant to -- I mean to deal with -- with this issue because it's very important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, were you able to find out which of these detention facilities were open later than 1992? Oh, I'm sorry, in Bijeljina. In Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: In Bijeljina. Very well, then. I made some notes of some dates. Batkovic was open from July 1992 to June 1995; Novo Selo, 1993; Patkovaca, 1994; Vanek's mill, 1993; the school S. Haso, 1993; Osman Velagic School in 1993. Those were the places that were opened after 1992 and became detention centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to ask you again to slow down if you give -- especially if you give names and numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may, I would suggest, because it's -- I can see for -- for transcription is very difficult to catch the names. If you always could refer rather to the number, which means -- you mentioned Patkovaca. It's 2.8. So if you could slowly now repeat with the number of that detention facility and say that -- when it was open.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Are you -- are you referring only to those that were opened in 1993 and later, and are these the ones that you want me to mention?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. If you could repeat it with -- with numbers assigned to these detention places.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: 2.4, Bijeljina SUP, from June 1992 until December 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mrs. Malesevic. Only those who were open after 1993.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: 2.6, Janja Field, 1993; 2.7, Novo Selo agricultural combine, May 1993; 2.10, Patkovaca, in January 1994; Vanek's mill, 2.13, April 1993 until December 1993; 2.14, S. Haso school from December 1993 until December 1994; 2.15, Osman Velagic's house, January 1993 to December 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we have Bileca municipality. We listed five places. To your knowledge, were all these places detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our documentation, all the five places are considered places of detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they all open and operated in 1992 or were they -- some opened in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our records, all were opened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bosanska Krupa. We listed six places, and again, to your knowledge, were they all places of detention?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our information, Bosanska Krupa had five detention places. 4.3, the elementary school, we don't have any documents for that place, and we therefore did not consider it a detention place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that all these places were open in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to our information, between the 21st of April and 17 September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have further Bosanski Novi, where we listed 11 places. Did you -- did you find all of them in -- in -- are they all places of detention?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that one place of detention appears here under two different names; that's 5.5 and 5.7. The two are actually one and the same place of detention. Japra, the Japra company, according to our documents, is a collections centre; Blagaj was a detention centre where private houses were used to detain inmates, and that's why we considered it a detention centre. All the places were opened in 1992 and closed in 1992, save for Suha Medja, which was the separation line that was in the front where the inmates were taken as work force, and they were digging trenches there, and they were kept there. According to our documentation, this place of detention was opened in 1992 and remained a place of detention until the end of the war, and I now see the elementary school in Bosanski Novi, which was also a collection centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Bosanski Petrovac, we listed nine places. Are they all -- were they, all these places, detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to our records, we consider all of them detention places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you agree that they all were open in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 1st of May, 1992, they were all opened and they were all active until the end of September of that same year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you confirm that Kamenica camp, under 6.3, is in fact in Titov Drvar but the people from Bosanski Novi -- from Bosanski Petrovac were taken there?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is between Petrovac and Drvar, and most of the inmates came from Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bratunac, we listed nine places. Were they all detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would just like to say that 7.2, the football stadium in Bratunac, and 7.5, stadium, is one and the same place of deposition. Also, 7.1, Bjelovac, that was actually the place of a massacre. People were brought there and executed there, according to our documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that 7.7 and 7.8 were, in fact, open only in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our documents, on the 12th of July these detention places were opened and they were active until the 17th of July. This is -- this surrounds the time of the events in Srebrenica. The others were opened in 1992 and closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask the witness: You're referring to the 12th and the 17th of July. That's 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1995, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Brcko, we listed 16 places. Were they all detention places in accordance with -- with your records?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Based on our documentation, I cannot confirm 8.10, the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: The other places, according to our documents, were indeed places of detention. All these places were opened on the 1st of May, 1992, and closed during the same year. But Luka, the barracks, and the MUP kept functioning until the end of the war. Only small groups were brought to those detention places; however, they were active and we have documents to prove that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And demolished villas in Potocari, 8.16, was opened only in 1995; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, yes, correct. That was in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In ^ajni~e we have three detention -- we have three places. To your knowledge, were they all detention facilities, and were they all open in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our information, all the three were detention places. They were all opened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Celinac, we have four places; however, is it correct that 10.3 and 10.4 -- I'm sorry. We have four places. Are they all detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: In Celinac, according to our information, the first three were detention places, but the bank in Celinac under 10.4, we do not have any valid documents to prove that. All of these places were opened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doboj. In Doboj, there are 30 places. Were they all places of detention, according to your records?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, 11.1, the 4th of July Barracks, and the Miljackovac Barracks are one and the same place. 11.28, Vinjska, we don't have documents that prove that this was a place of detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that 11.29 and 11.30 were opened in 1993 and all others were opened in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According our documents, Majevac was opened between 10 of June and 10 of November, 1992, and the -- 1993. The rest were opened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologies for not having heard the -- all of the information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Usora warehouse, the central prison, was active until the end of the war. Small groups of detainees were brought to those places.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I heard that we didn't hear something or the interpreters were not able to -- to interpret it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you said "according to our documents, Majevac was opened between 10th of July and 10th of November, 1992," and then you said something about 1993, but the interpreters missed what followed and your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. 11.30, Ozren Kersten was the place of detention, which was opened the 10th of November, 1993, and closed on the 6th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Majevac opened in 1992 or in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Majevac was opened on the 10th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we can move to Donji Vakuf, in which we have 12 places. Is it correct that -- that all were detention facilities, or did you find that some of them wouldn't be a place of detention?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: After the analysis, 12.1, Djurda Kuce in Donji Vakuf, we could not confirm that this was a place of detention. The rest, according to our documentation, were detention places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that all of them were opened in 1992, apart from 12.12, which was opened only in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of these places were opened in 1992 except for number 12.12, which was opened in 1995, which -- this was opened to receive inmates from Mrkonjic Grad. They spent only several days there, and when the place was being closed, 27 out of the 28 inmates were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Foca. In Foca, we have 24 places. Did you find that some of them wouldn't be a detention facility?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, we have different names for the same place. The school centre in Srednja, 13.1, and 13.2, the secondary school, this is just one place. Also, number 13.3, Karaman's house, and 13.5, the women's camp in a private house, that is also one place. Number 13.6 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just -- I notice you said 13.5, and you were referring to female camp in Miljevina. Is it correct that it is 13.15?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: 13.3, Karaman's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 13.15 are the same place?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: 13.15 is the same as 13.3. Also, according to our documentation, we cannot confirm 13.5, the restaurant across the road from the prison. We don't have documents to prove that. Also, we don't have documents to prove 13.16, Podedze. I don't have any information about that place of detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- and is it correct that all other places were found in -- in your records as detention facilities, and they were all opened in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our information, they were all opened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Gacko. We have six places. Were they all detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our information, they were all detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that some work was done for you by either cantonal associations or municipal associations. I received a list of detention facilities from the Canton Sarajevo Association of Concentration Camp inmates. And is it correct that you cooperated and they collected all this information, which you later verified?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Sarajevo canton belongs to the alliance of inmates of Bosnia and Herzegovina. For certain financial reasons, they took it upon themselves to do that part of the job, to list the camps and check them. The Sarajevo canton made a list of all the camps and forwarded this to you. In the alliance, we don't have enough workforce to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to -- to tender these two documents. One is dated 16 of June, 2005, and the ERN number is 0423- 0146.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P886.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The other one is dated 21st of June, 2005, and the ERN number is 0423-0146.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Is there a B/C/S version of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In fact, you can see that the -- the detention facilities or the places are in both languages. One is in B/C/S, and the other one is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And just for the information of Mr. Krajisnik, the heading only clarifies who sent it, to whom it was sent, and that it is a list of detention facilities in Canton Sarajevo in 1992 and then splits that up in Vogosca, Pale, and Trnovo. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In this case, I would like to rely on this list for the municipalities Hadzici, Ilidza, Novo Sarajevo, Novi Grad, Ilijas, Vogosca, and Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Malesevic, I would like to continue with the municipality of Kalinovik. For Kalinovik, the Prosecution listed seven places. To your knowledge, were they all places of detention and were they all open in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our information, only 18.1, the school in Ulog, we are not sure whether this was a detention camp or a collection centre. So 18.1, I cannot confirm. As for the rest of them, we have documentation that proves that they were detention centres, and they were all opened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For municipality of Kljuc, we listed seven places, and is it correct that they were all places of detention and they were all open in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: In Kljuc, the only disputable thing is 19.7, the school in Biljani. We don't know exactly how long the inmates were there; we know that it was a massacre place, where they were killed. The rest were detention centres. Although, the school in Biljani was intended to be a detention facility, all the people were taken there against the law, and they were all executed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they all in -- were they all open in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were all opened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I can see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We -- it's a quarter to 2.00. Just for scheduling purposes, Ms. Richterova, could you give us any impression on how much time you'd still need from now on?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will only finish the remaining municipalities, and there are - if I can count - there are about seven of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it takes quite some time. Mr. Josse, could you give us any indication on how much time you would approximately need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I said half an hour yesterday. I'm going to be at least half an hour, I think nearer three-quarters of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So there's no way that we'll finish now. We'll resume at 3.00 this afternoon, and to the extent possible, we might be able to finish in one session. We'll adjourn until then. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber -- or rather, the Presiding Judge apologizes for the late start.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should just say Your Honour will see Mr. Stewart is not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm informed about --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- his presence nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Richterova, would you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Malesevic, before the adjournment, we left the municipality of Kljuc. Another municipality is Kotor Varos, where we listed 17 places. First, I want to say that we inadvertently added two places under 20.16 and 20.17, which do not belong to the municipality of Kotor Varos but to the municipality of Celinac, and they were dealt with, which left -- which leave us with 15 places. Mrs. Malesevic, can you confirm that all these places are places -- were places of detention and they were all open in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Before I answer the question, I have to say that 20.1 and 20.15 was one place. Fourteen places in Kotor Varos. According to our records, all were open in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only want to make a small correction in the transcript. The witness was referring to 20.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other municipality is Nevesinje, where we listed six places. And again, were all these places, places of detention and open in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Well, with Konjic, we have 21, 20. It is the camp at Boracko Lake, which belongs to Konjic, and 21.6, the basement in Kucevo [phoen]. That belongs to the Konjic municipality. That means places of detention in Nevesinje equals four, and we have documentation to bear that out. Oh, I apologise. We have 21.4, the factory, and 21.5, the workshop. That is one detention place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then -- and can you confirm that they were all open in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were all open in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you are asking about 1992, could you put the same question to the witness in request of Gacko because there it was not done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if we could quickly return to the municipality of Gacko, where we listed six places of detention. Were they all open in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our records, yes, they were all open in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another municipality is Prijedor, in which we listed 58 places. Can you confirm that, in fact, only five of them, which is police station in Prijedor, command post at Miska Glava -- I'm sorry, police station in Prijedor - that's 25.2 - command post at Miska Glava, 25.3; Omarska, 25.4; Keraterm, 25.5; and Trnopolje, 25.6 were detention centres. The remaining places were just collection centres or collection points; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When it comes to collection centres or points, there was a dilemma with us. Yes, we did list this under collection centres; however, those collection centres lasted for several days sometimes. The people had been collected there, and they were mistreated, abused there, basic human rights withheld. However, the other five places were defined as places of detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct to state that all these places were open or functional in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to our records, they were all opened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The municipality of Rogatica: we have ten places. Can you confirm whether, yes or no, all were places of detention?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me mention that 26.1, the secondary school in Rogatica, and 26.6, the Veljko Vlahovic school in Rogatica, is one place of detention. Also, 26.4, the square in Rogatica, we don't have any information about that particular place of detention; whereas, all the rest were places of detention. I beg your pardon. 26.9, the Podgoj, we have no information about that, that it was a detention centre, either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they all open in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our records, yes, they were all open in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the municipality of Rudo, we listed two places. Were both of them in -- can you find both of them in your records?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our records, yes, two places; the barracks and the recreational centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they open in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were also open in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the municipality of Sanski Most, we listed 22 places. Were they all detention centres?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our records, this number is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find any duplications, the same place which would be indicated under more than one place?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: In Sanski Most, no remarks of that kind. It's all properly defined and done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that 25.16, Stari Majdan, was open in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to our records, Stari Majdan was opened only in 1995, as well as the boiler room of the Sanas Hotel [phoen]. According to our records, that was opened on the 16th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is 28.18. And is it also correct that 28.19, Sekovci, and 28.20, Trnova, were open in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's right. These places were subsequently opened in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then again, for the record, Ms. Richterova, where it said 25.16, it should also be 28.16, Stari Majdan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that all the -- yes. And is it correct that all other places were open in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our information, the rest were opened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The municipality of Sipovo: we listed only one place. Do you have any records for detention facilities in the Sipovo municipality?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our records, Sipovo SUP is only mentioned. Nothing else. No other records in Sipovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it open as a detention centre in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to our records, in 1992. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The municipality of Sokolac, there are ten places. Were they all places of detention according to your records?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our records, all the places were places of detention, yes, and also opened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the place under 30.9 is, in fact, a private house in Cavarina instead of Cavarlija?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Cavarina, yes. There's a mistake there. Cavarina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 30.6, winter road maintenance point, is it correct that this point was used in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to our records, that was used as a place of detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1993? The question was whether to your knowledge it was in 1993 or 1992.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our records, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As well as all other places mentioned under Sokolac; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Teslic, we listed 18 places; however, at the beginning I would like to state that we inadvertently added places which belong to the municipality of Doboj, and I am talking about places under 31.12 to 31.18. It leaves us with 11 places in the municipality of Teslic. Were -- were they all places of detention?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our records, all the places were considered places of detention, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they all open in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all the places were open in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that 31.1 is the same as 31.8?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've just noticed that myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that 31.3 is the same as 31.6?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have in your records Mladost School, which is under 31.5?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all these places were open in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Vlasenica, we listed 17 places. To your knowledge, were they all places of detention?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our information, 32.5, the stadium at Vlasenica, was a collection centre. 32.7, the playground in Kasaba, was the site of an execution; that's where a massacre took place. Otherwise, all of them were open in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this massacre which took place on a playground on -- in Kasaba, when did it take place?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I have the exact date somewhere but not -- it doesn't seem to be here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that it was in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't note the date, I'm afraid. I just -- what I have noted is that it was an execution site. I would have to check that out subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you at least know whether it was after 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was after 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last municipality is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova, in Vlasenica also a Camp Luka appears; whereas, we had in Brcko Luka camp. It's not the same, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Camp Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could ask the witness. We see that a camp with a similar name appears in Vlasenica, and that is a different camp from Luka Camp in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not the same one. No. This is the name of a village between Srebrenica and Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That sufficiently clarifies my doubt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Zvornik municipality, there were 26 places listed. To your knowledge, were they all places of detention?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our information, 34.16, the stadium at Divic, was a collection centre, and also 34.24, Orahovac Karakaj, was also a collection centre. All the rest may be considered as places of detention according to our information and records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they all open in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: According to our records, they were all open in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we add up all these places, we -- we will have approximately 300 detention facilities in these 34 municipalities. When you testified last time, you stated that there were 651 registered camps, which -- and 520 were under Serb control. Do you still stand for this information?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said last time. But in the meantime, the information may have changed because we are still gathering information about places of detention, so it is possible that new places of detention might have been registered in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, this number refers to the period -- this number 651 refers to the period 1992 to 1995; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. I don't have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give you the opportunity to cross-examine the witness, Mr. Josse, Judge Hanoteau would have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask the witness to tell me what she means by "the massacre site." Does that mean that there were people who were held there and that they were all massacred, or what? Or was it a site where prisoners were taken to be massacred? Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say it was an execution site, I referred to the fact that a group of people were killed there; that it was not a place where people were detained for a long time and gradually taken off one by one to be killed, but that, rather, they were all killed in one day, for example, all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't a place where there were people who were detained and killed, assassinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we don't count this as a place of detention but as a place of execution; however, we list them, as we do collection centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I terribly apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I be allowed to ask one more question, just to clarify one -- one point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- let's do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we were talking about these detention facilities, can you -- can you tell us, based on your knowledge, who were people detained in these facilities? What was the ethnicity of people who were detained there?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I will say that we collect information on detainees and inmates regardless of their ethnic and religious affiliation, so it all depends on who was in control of the place of detention and who was detained there. Unfortunately, there were camps on all three sides. But I think that today we are only referring to camps under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in these Serb-controlled detention facilities, are you able to -- to tell us who were -- which ethnicity were the detained people?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: In the places of detention under Serb control, it was non-Serbs Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who were detained. Mostly Croats and Bosniaks. There were even small numbers of Serbs.
