These were people who refused to go to the war theatre or for whatever reason, so that there were also Serbs but a small number of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would have another question, as well, Mr. Josse. There's a lot I would ask for you, in terms of patience. The Chamber has had an opportunity, although it's not in evidence, to read a statement, a witness statement you gave in October 2001. It's a relatively short statement in which is contained a table of camps. One of the items seems to be under whose authorities these detention camps or detention centres are held, and it mainly says "Serb authorities," with a few exceptions, in view of Omarska and in view of Keraterm, for example. We see that the list mentions "SDS, Serb authorities." Are these two places of detention, Omarska and Keraterm, different, in view of you, in terms of under whose control they were, where you at least give a different denomination of the controlling party or authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's an individual interpretation by the witness. I think there are no differences between Omarska, Keraterm, Rasadnik [phoen], or any other camp. They were all under the control of the Serb forces. However, the interviewees wrote down what they thought was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you are not in a position to say that these were different. It's just you did write down what they said, and you did not give it any follow-up as to further inquiry into that matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. We didn't go into it any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then a final question. Ms. Richterova, you've asked the witness about the ethnicity of those kept in detention centres. I didn't hear anything as to their status, in terms of military or civilian. Was it on purpose that you didn't ask for it? Are you informed that there's no information about it, or ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It was not on purpose. It's possible that I omitted to ask this question, but nowhere I found any information on -- on this. So if I am allowed to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're allowed to complete the examination-in- chief in this respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Malesevic, when you kept the records of people who were detained, did you also pay attention to the status of these people, whether they were civilians or whether they were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Of course we paid attention to that. A very small number of these people were arrested on a battlefield, and these are marked as such. But the vast majority of the people were civilians, women, children, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able -- able to give us at least a percentage of those who were kept as soldiers? Who were caught as soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that at present because I don't have this information at hand, but I can tell you that it was a very small number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse. Cross-examined by Mr. Josse:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Malesevic, I'd also like to ask you about the ethnicity of your organisation. Who funds it, first of all, please?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: After it was founded, nobody took over the foundation. For one period, the government of the Federation set aside some funds which were insufficient. As far as I know, nobody is funding it at present. What we did was we engaged in publishing activities so as to earn something to cover our minimum expenses, and then we also have membership fees, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And membership fees are paid by the former inmates; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only those who can pay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in terms of cooperation from the different ethnic groups that make up Bosnia and Herzegovina, has there been equal cooperation from all the ethnic parties?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question. Are you referring to the camp inmates?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me -- yes, I am referring to the camp inmates, if that makes it clear.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I can say that while I was active in the association, we did have cooperation. We have much in common; for example, the status of inmates at the level of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We cooperated with camp inmates from the Republika Srpska and camp inmates from the Croatian part, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because I was going to suggest that you don't get the cooperation from those people who live in the Republika Srpska, Serbs in particular. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I can only speak of the period in which I was active. In certain segments, for example, demands made to the government to resolve our status issues, we did have joint action. Apart from that, the Association of Camp Inmates drew up information on human rights violations from 1992 to 1995. This was done jointly, and it was forwarded to the ministry. And the cooperation was, in fact, much better than expected in this respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you told us that your organisation was formed as a result of there being a number of similar organisations, and the National Alliance was an umbrella group; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was at the level of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that the information gathered at municipal level could be brought together in one place, for purposes of research and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard of a man called Jovocic - I'll spell that if I may: J-o-v-i-c-i-c-h - who is the vice-president of a Serbian camp inmates group who was detained for a time in Tarcin prison?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Not only have I heard of him, but I have met Mr. Jovocic personally, and we cooperated together. What I can say, however, is that the Association of Camp Inmates of Republika Srpska has more prisoners of war than the association we represent, which represents, for the most part, civilians, and there were some small misunderstandings in this respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is noticeable that in the statement to which the learned Judge, Judge Orie, referred you to a few moments ago, as far as I can see, the only Bosnian authority institution listed is, in fact, Tarcin prison, at page 9, being item 8, in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I have to say in this list of camps we have lists for 37 municipalities, and there are camps here which are missing that were under Croatian control and so on, and maybe the young woman who drew up this list omitted to put in Tarcin. But it was only for these 37 municipalities that information was requested, which is why the list looks the way it does. But I think in this case, it was an omission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to be unfair in relation to that. In fact, we've got the two additional documents, the one that has ERN number 04230148; that includes Tarcin, to be fair. I don't know whether you've got that there.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. This is what I was talking about a little while ago. The colleague who was drawing up the list for the Sarajevo canton - and we were dealing with camps under Serb control, as does Annex C - I assume it was an omission. There is, however, a list of all camps, regardless of whose control they were under, and there you can find both Tarcin and Celebici and Fikret Abdic's camps, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me my ignorance. Where were they, the two -- the last two you mentioned? Were they -- were they in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Tarcin was under Bosniak control, and it is on the territory of the Sarajevo canton. Celebici was in Konjic; it was also under Bosniak control. I mentioned this for the sake of illustration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And I want to ask you about Sarajevo. What information did your organisation obtain about people who were detained within Sarajevo during the course of the siege of that city?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question because I think that at present we do not have this information available. The Association of Camp Inmates is a voluntary organisation. People join it voluntarily and volunteer to make their statements about detention sites. I have no information that there were such sites. I am not saying they didn't exist; I am just saying that nobody came forward to tell us about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you specifically about -- and again, excuse me my pronunciation - I'll spell it, if need be, but I think most people in this courtroom are very familiar with this place - the Viktor Bubanj Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: The Viktor Bubanj Barracks, as far as I know, was a traditional type of jail. There were Serbs detained there, also 150 Bosniaks who had been charged with crimes or had refused the mobilisation call. I was interested in the Viktor Bubanj Barracks because of a colleague, Jovocic. There were people of various ethnicities detained there and detained for various reasons. That's what I know about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware of a controversy that has arisen as to whether a plaque commemorating those who were detained there could be placed at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am aware of it. But I cannot answer a question about it because in Bosnia and Herzegovina there was no law on plaques. There is no legislation defining such places officially, and that is why there was a confrontation between camp inmates from the Republika Srpska and camp inmates who live in Sarajevo. We did not want to come into conflict with the authorities. I've told you what I knew about the Viktor Bubanj Barracks; if it is confirmed that it was a camp for Serbs, then nobody will object to their commemorating this in an appropriate way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's very helpful, madam. You've answered my follow-up question. It -- when you talk about "we," you mean the organisation you represent?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I am referring to the camp inmates of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not entirely clear to me where you were referring to when you were referring to "we," Mr. Josse. The last part of the answer of the witness was about nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought I heard the word "we." It's not on the transcript; I readily accept that. Perhaps I should clarify the matter. I'm anxious to. I thought I'd move on, not to waste any more time, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am anxious to clarify the matter if I will be permitted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the matter is -- I have no need for clarification. If, of course, the witness said something else, that should be checked on the tape. But I didn't fully understand the question, as a matter of fact, what you were referring to, but the answer of the witness is such that would satisfy me as an answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you next about Prijedor. If we could look at Prijedor in the list that you've got there, please, and I want to ask you in particular about 25.6. You've told us that 25.6, as far as your records are concerned, was, in fact, a detention centre; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us on what information you base that? Because I suggest you're mistaken and that place was only a collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I have to repeat: A place of detention in our view is every place where civilians were brought by force and were -- where terror was exercised over them, where they were beaten up, maltreated, and so on. As for Trnopolje, it was active until a certain period. And throughout those seven days, there were murders, there were rapes, beatings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: One murder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The people who were in Trnopolje at the time bore witness to torture. That is what this is based on, the fact that Trnopolje is listed as a detention centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And presumably offhand you'd be unable to tell us how many of your members were detained at that particular place.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: In Trnopolje? I can't say precisely how many of our members were there, but I think it was about 800 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd also like to deal specifically with Pale, if I may, Ms. Malesevic. Again, the documents that were referred to earlier - this time it's ERN 04230146 that I'm referring to - lists detention facilities that it's suggested were in Pale in 1992. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: With Their Honours' leave, I've already said that I myself did not prepare this document on Pale; it was my colleague, Ms. Muratcaus. So I would beg not to have to answer this question because it wasn't I personally who made this list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You did say that, and I didn't appreciate that fully. You've -- you've explained that you've left the organisation. We see that this document is dated June of this year. That's presumably why she prepared it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're -- you're therefore not able to answer any questions about Pale. I say that because I have some very specific instructions about detention centres in Pale, but if you're not able to deal with them, there's no point, subject to anything the learned Judge says, my putting these matters to you. It's right, you've got no knowledge about Pale; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no personal knowledge about Pale detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would prefer not to answer questions about Pale because I have not prepared for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say you might have information available to you, but it's not, I would say, actively in your memory at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would the same be true, madam, of Novi Grad?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's also in the Sarajevo canton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Two -- two or three other matters. It's right, as you've told us -- and I don't want to dwell on this. But you were detained by Croatian forces, Croatian civilians? What was it? If you don't want to say, I understand, and I will not pursue this line. I really will understand, and I will withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: There's no reason for me not to answer. I was arrested by the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And detained by, effectively, police, rather than soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: The police, yes. But I must add that the police arrested me in Kresevo. After Jajce was taken over by the Serb army, I found myself in Kresevo as a refugee, and several months later the police arrested us, like the other Bosniaks, in Kresevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you've said in your statement that initially you were detained with Serbs but that they were released before you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. A certain number of Serbs were captured by the Croatian police, and after some time, they were left and we were kept there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think possibly -- I hope my last topic, Ms. Malesevic, relates to compensation. Is the organisation, the Alliance, fighting for compensation in any way for former inmates?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. That was one of the priorities when the Alliance of Inmates was established. We tried to do so through the law, but it was very difficult. And the question is still open today; it hasn't been solved. Then we took the decision at the second congress that we held collectively to appeal for compensation, that is to say, material remuneration, and that process is ongoing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, if you can explain this simply, who are inmates to look to for compensation?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: The civilian inmates who lost their jobs, lost all their property, movable and immovable, and that have suffered heavy psychophysical consequences. They've lost their jobs, as I said, and so on and so forth. And in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they don't have any rights, even the right to treatment, medical treatment. So this was a way to draw attention to that whole group of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What I wanted to know is who was going to pay compensation to former inmates or who it's hoped will pay compensation to former inmates.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: To -- it was paid by the state, the entity to war -- to the POWs, but not to civilians. So perhaps that is part of the question and my answer with respect to Jovicic, perhaps it is easier for them because they could have received some remuneration from their organisations. But we're civilians, so there's nobody we can address this to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that still remains the status at the moment? The civilians don't have anyone to address their claim for compensation to?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there any talk from the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina to set up some sort of compensation fund?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last matter is this: I've noticed, unfortunately, I don't think this document has been circulated in the bundle that has been handed out, but I think we can deal with it like this. It's right that there is something called the Rules on Establishing the Status of Camp Prisoners of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated November of 2000? Do you know what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. In fact, they are rules on establishing the status of camp prisoners of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is one of the basic documents of the alliance. It has undergone certain amendments since it was established, but it regulates the rules and regulations according to who can be a member, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your original statement, you also annexed - I think originally it was at tab 5 of that statement - something called Research and Documentation Centre Sarajevo, project, classification of places of imprisonment of the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and forms of torture during the war 1992 to 1995. Are you aware of what I'm talking about there?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Without the text -- that was a key project of the Alliance of Inmates of Bosnia and Herzegovina, first of all on the basis of which we list all the places of detention and describe them, and we were going to hold an international conference after that for verification. At the level of the state, this should be done. We expected once it came into force or came into being -- we thought the status of inmates would be speeded up, the settlement of their status, and we discussed this from our colleagues of the RES. They were also interested in this, and I think that the project will be completed at some point in time in the future.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the document is a very admirable setting-out of the project plan. At number 1 on the second page of the document, it says this: "All nations and national minorities were victims of war, but the number of Bosniaks show that they have suffered a very heavy form of war crime. That is qualified as genocide according to the international standards." Did you have any part in putting that particular sentence in the document?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: In a way. Well, you caught me unawares now, but it was teamwork. But at any case, that is how it stands. That is what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that - and correct me if I'm wrong, Ms. Malesevic, of course - exactly the type of statement that is going to effectively put Serbs off cooperating with your organisation?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I might not have understood your question. Can the truth divide us? Everything we're doing, I think we're doing to draw closer together and to live together. So I'm afraid I might have misunderstood you. But when it comes to genocide, the word was uttered, and that was at this Tribunal, and I think that's normal. So we have to tell the truth, regardless of who the perpetrators were, which ethnic group, which nation was responsible, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you -- you didn't understand me, and I say thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Krajisnik, would you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honours. I have no questions for this lady.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have only one clarification. Re-examined by Ms. Richterova:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Malesevic, when the Defence counsel asked you about Trnopolje, you said, "And throughout the seven days," such-and-such things happened. Did you really say during seven days?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I think it's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what were you -- which period of time were you referring to? Talking about Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to Trnopolje, Trnopolje was active from May to December. I haven't got any notes, though. All this must be taken with a few reservations. But I know from the reports I read and the witness is testifying about the crimes, the torture and abuse, that Trnopolje was truly a camp, a place of detention according to all our parameters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There might be some confusion. Let me see whether I can clarify it. When you said, "And throughout those seven days," did you have some specific seven days in mind, or did you want to refer to seven days a week, just as we say 24 hours a day; that means full time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I meant the specific statement, where it said, "seven days of torture, abuse," and so on. That's the last portion I read in preparing for my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: That's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Canivell has one or more questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to make clear that when you said that places in which people were executed, you called them sites of execution, when all the persons detained there were executed or even if some of the persons retained or detained there survived, wasn't put to execution?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: The execution sites that we denoted as such according to witness testimony, all the people were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Another point I would like to know: You have taken into consideration facts like the -- some of the people that were detained in one location were later perhaps transferred to other places, and so in the way that perhaps I wondered if you would be able to make a calculation of the total amount of people that had been detained in these camps under the Serbian authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we still do not have the exact figures, but it is common knowledge that from Omarska, the camp -- the inmates were taken to Manjaca and 400 to Batkovici on from there. So when we deal with all the places and all the people passing through those places of detention, we'll be able to see that they are three places and see the number of people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Another point is: Had you been able to establish a correlation between the number of people detained in every municipality in relation with the number of Muslims living in those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your question. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: I mean, if you had discovered if in every municipality, every different municipality, the number of people detained was similar that other places or you found that taking into consideration the number of Muslims living in every municipality, the number of the people detained were higher or lower in one or the others.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't perform analysis of that kind, but the assumption is that it was proportionately the same, with respect to the total number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: There's another question I would like to pose to you: Would you be able to say that the higher number of detained people was around 1992, later on, or when?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: 1992 was the year when there were most number of detainees. After that, they either moved out or were moved out, but 1992 was the peak year when the largest numbers of the population were detained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Could you -- had you been able to find differences on the ways people finished their stay in these camps? I mean, for instance, how much people, what proportion of those people were killed, were released, were exchanged, were liberated? You have had any calculation about that?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: I do, but not right with me here. But I'll try and give you an illustration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask you: I see that you're consulting a document. Could you tell us what document you are consulting so that we know. Are these personal notes, or is this...?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: May I show it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, no, that's clear. It's the schedule, that has been -- Schedule C that has been presented to you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Schedule C. What I can tell you is this: We're talking about camps where they were killed en masse. For example, the KP Dom in Foca. Of the 700 detainees, 322 were killed. In Vuk Karadzic school of Bratunac, about 700 detainees there and about 400 were killed, and so on. The gunpowder warehouse, for instance. Well, I haven't prepared myself for that, but in some places of detention, like Prijedor and Omarska, people were liquidated en masse. Celopek is another case in point, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Were people that were put in Omarska or Trnopolje or other of those more numerous where people were detained were brought from other locations in different municipalities to be there and later on had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MELIKA MALESEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps from the surrounding villages: Kljuc, Sanski Most. But otherwise, it was the local inhabitants in the case of Prijedor. Whereas, Batkovici, the inmates were from all over Bosnia-Herzegovina, just like Manjaca, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since Judge Hanoteau has no questions for you, neither do I. I first ask the parties whether the questions of Judge Canivell have triggered any need to further --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not from the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Ms. Malesevic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and to answer the questions of the parties and the questions put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort Ms. Malesevic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could we go through the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova, no statement has been tendered of the witness, although it's on the list, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm just -- I would like to tender this statement dated 15 and 16 of October 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, this is a bit late. So the Defence only now, although they could have known that, Ms. Richterova, had them on the list of potential exhibits. But in cross-examination they could have refrained from certain questions because they thought that the statement was not in evidence. Therefore, I specifically ask whether there's any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I have one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm glad to say Mr. Stewart and I are of the same mind, which is this: I have no objection in relation to this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The -- these statements, bearing in mind their contents, do not bother us, and we're happy for the Trial Chamber to have them. But this is no concession that in other circumstances our stance wouldn't be completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I already explained to Ms. Richterova that this is procedural -- not the proper course of action.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I apologise, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- that I didn't tender it at an earlier stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that should be the routine, at least if you want to tender. Now, if we're talking about statement or statements ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm referring only to one statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, one statement only. And that would be the October statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is a statement dated 15 and 16 October 2001 with the ERN number 0211-6884 to 6897.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Richterova. Madam Registrar, including this document, we would then have ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Since I hear no objections, they are admitted into evidence. I have one further observation for you, Mr. Josse: You put a question to the witness whether -- you put it to her, as a matter of fact, that Trnopolje was not a detention centre but, rather, a collection centre. You did not give it much follow-up when the witness explained that. The Defence is fully entitled to challenge any fact that is adopted as an adjudicated fact, but I wondered where the adjudicated facts say that thousands of prisoners were held, that armed soldiers guarded the camp, that the area -- an area - not the area but an area - of Trnopolje camp was surrounded by barbed wire, that there were more rapes at this camp than at any other camp, whether this approach would be the beginning of a challenging of adjudicated facts, especially where it's also part of the adjudicated facts that Trnopolje was at times, at least, an open prison, although it was dangerous for inmates to be found outside where they might be attacked by hostile groups in the neighbourhood, and this in effect amounted to imprisonment in the camp. I wondered whether under those circumstances -- of course, it could be the beginning of challenging that, but it was not perfectly clear to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will have to excuse my ignorance, but I'm not clear in the context of this Chamber and Tribunal what an adjudicated fact is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, an adjudicated fact is a fact which is established by another Chamber after the matter has been fully litigated. The parties can propose the Chamber to adopt adjudicated facts, which should be facts and not matters of law. And then after an exchange of views between the parties, the Chamber decides whether or not it will adopt that fact as an adjudicated fact, which does not mean that it's there forever but you'll also understand that, first of all, one of the consequences is that the Prosecution has no need to further prove that fact but, of course, the Defence is in a position to challenge the fact. But you'll also understand that if this fact has been established on the basis of a fully litigated -- in a fully litigated way, that it needs a bit more effort than just challenging another fact would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I say two things: First of all, I mean this very genuinely. I'm very grateful for Your Honour's explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And my apologies for not knowing that. Secondly, of course, I didn't -- it follows from what I've just asked Your Honour, I didn't know it was an adjudicated fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thirdly, though I'm not anxious to go into matters of privilege, clearly it was a result of a short conversation with Mr. Krajisnik. It may have been a misunderstanding on my part, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I have insufficient knowledge, as was quite clear, I fear, from the way I asked the questions, to pursue the matter any further. Whether it's something we're going to pursue further is something I will -- I see Mr. Krajisnik putting his hand up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that's something I need to discuss with him and Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, as a matter of fact, that you clearly said at that moment - but let me just - well, it was in my mind somewhere that you said that you were instructed. But I'll leave that apart. That's not something to be raised at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I'd ask like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- to just briefly say something. First of all, clearly I have absolutely no complaint about what Mr. Josse has just said because if it's anybody's responsibility to fill him in on what adjudicated facts were, it was mine. I'd just like to make it clear, Your Honour, I actually do believe I know what adjudicated facts are, but then I've been here rather a long time. But if I had done the cross-examination, there's no chance this issue would have come up because there's no chance I would have had enough time to explore that or unearth that adjudicated fact anyway, so Mr. Josse has covered the cross-examination at least as thoroughly as I would have done anyway. Because in the circumstances of this case, Your Honour, it is just impossible for the Defence team to follow these highways and byways in this matter. So -- well, there we are, Your Honour. That's the way it is. Your Honour has consistently said that -- something along the lines of perfection is not required, that a robust approach has to be adopted, Your Honour. Sometimes the robust approach has to be rather too robust in these circumstances, but I do wish to make that clear, Your Honour. It is simply impossible for us to do this, so these slight flaws in cross-examinations are going to emerge whether it's Mr. Josse, whether it's me, whether it's Ms. Loukas. It's absolutely inevitable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record, Mr. Stewart. I think, as a matter of fact, that I wanted to draw the attention to this specific issue, where I felt that it might not have been fully clear. Mr. Krajisnik, you'd like to add something? The Chamber is aware that how free people were to leave or not to leave Trnopolje is a matter that has been in other cases extensively dealt with. Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think you've explained it all, more or less. However, I wish to be fair. I completely forgot about adjudicated facts. I suggested to Mr. Josse that Trnopolje was an open collection centre and that he should note that. And, in fact, it is our intention to prove that in our case, so that it's not Mr. Josse's fault, if I can put it that way, because I didn't know about the adjudicated facts and the procedure linked to that. I just wanted to show what we were going to prove to the Court in due course. So thank you for giving us your explanations. That is the legal explanations. It is a legal matter, and it is not quite along the lines of what I thought as being the subject of discussion in future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, all being on the right track again, is there any other procedural issue to be raised at this moment? Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly. On Monday, the Prosecution will seek approximately 15 minutes, I would estimate, to raise matters in connection with the cross-examination of Witness Davidovic. I raise that for two reasons: Number one, for the simple -- to foreshadow a simple scheduling matter; and number two, because he was Mr. - - or he was Ms. Loukas's witness, and I have been advised that she may not be planning to be present next week or during the remainder of the case. I wanted to raise it so that the Defence would have an opportunity to alert her if she did want to be present for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I think, Your Honour, in fact Ms. Loukas -- she will be here, anyway, on Monday because she is handling Mr. Brown. What Mr. Tieger says applies beyond Mr. Brown. But -- but Ms. Loukas is taking Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then I raised it for a simple scheduling reason in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I would remind the Court that today, as has been our recent history, is dossier day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we would like therefore to tender the Zvornik dossier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Zvornik dossier. And then I take it it will be physically distributed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's there. Until now, the dossier, of course, most important is that Madam Registrar receives directly a copy. But usually the other copies find their way to those interested. The provisional number to be assigned to it would be, Madam Registrar ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Zvornik dossier will be Prosecution Exhibit P889.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Any other issue, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any issue to be raised by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then adjourn until next Monday, quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom, number 1.
